newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO says armed Moslems enter Bosnia village.
newsitem.headline: NATO says armed Moslems enter Bosnia village.

text.p: NATO officers voiced concern on Sunday over a group of about 100 Moslems carrying banned weapons into a ruined village in Serb-held territory for a second day.

Russian soldiers serving in the NATO-led peace implementation force (IFOR) confiscated an automatic rifle and several hand grenades from the Moslem men, who said they wanted to repair their homes in the village of Jusici in eastern Bosnia, an IFOR spokesman said.
Bosnian government television denied on Sunday night that the Moslem men were armed, saying they had discovered hunting rifles and grenades in the ruined village.
Avdo Hebib, interior minister for the Moslem-Croat federation, said the Moslems had a right to return to their village. "Who in the world would dare to tell them to leave their village?" Hebib said.

The village, almost totally destroyed during the Bosnian war, lies in the "zone of separation" near former front lines where submachine guns and other weapons are banned under terms of the Dayton peace agreement.
The Moslems entered the village on Saturday and Sunday but so far no violence has erupted despite protests from Serb authorities, Major Brett Boudreau said.
"They are military age men and they are bringing in weapons with them," Boudreau told Reuters. "At this stage it seems a little too coincidental...We will monitor the situation carefully," he added.
A similar incident last month led to a violent confrontation when Moslem men entered the nearby village of Mahala.
Bosnian Serb police armed with pistols and clubs attacked the Moslems and IFOR ultimately blamed both sides. Boudreau said the Serb police around Jusici had been restrained so far.
IFOR told Moslem-Croat federation authorities to come up with a list of those who owned property in the formerly Moslem village to determine who had a legitimate right to return.

NATO officers want Serb and federation interior ministers to agree a framework for Moslems trying to visit their pre-war homes. But the presence of the Moslem men in Jusici had derailed a meeting scheduled on Saturday.
